title: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings
hookLine: jeea jant ke thaakuraa: Lord of all beings, pervading all (Sukhmani 22)

lines: THE LORD OF EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.
cards: A single ant on the kitchen counter, walking a careful line toward a grain of sugar. The usual reflex is a paper towel, or a thumb. But stop and actually watch it, and it's remarkable.
It's carrying something heavier than itself. It's checking the way with its antennae. It's going somewhere, for some reason that matters to it.
The twenty-second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming the Lord of that ant, and of everything else that breathes.

teach.b: The salok, in paraphrase: Lord and Master of all beings and creatures, You Yourself are present in all of them. Nanak says: the One is spread out everywhere; where could a second be seen? Start with jeea jant.

Jeea are living beings, things with life and breath. Jant are creatures, every kind of animal. Together it's Gurbani's way of saying everyone and everything alive: people, ants, birds, fish, the cat on the windowsill.
Thaakur is lord or master, a word of respect for the one in charge. So the salok begins: Master of every living thing. But the second half changes what master means.
God isn't pictured as a landlord far off, collecting rent.
Aape vartanhaar: God Himself is the one moving within them all, present and active in each.

teach.h: EKO PASARIAA: THE ONE, SPREAD OUT.
teach.b: Then the last line: eko pasariaa. The One has spread out. Where is there a second to see?
This is one root of the respect Sikh teaching shows to living things. If the same One is spread through every creature, the ant on the counter isn't simply a pest or a stranger.
In the salok's picture, it's kin: made by the same Master, filled by the same presence. This isn't a rule about every mosquito. It means the glance you give a living thing can carry a little respect.
The ashtpadi begins by widening the circle of who counts.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi begin with a salok naming God the Master of all living beings, the One spread through every creature.

o: a landowner far off who collects rent
a temple's keeper who tends the shrine
lord and master, here of every living thing

s: the salok pictures God as a distant landlord
aape vartanhaar: God is the one moving within all beings.
jeea jant means every living thing, people and animals
Gurbani's way of saying everything alive.
the salok says there is a second power beside the One
it asks: the One is spread everywhere; where could a second be seen?

games.q: an ant crosses your counter. by the twenty-second salok, what is it?
o: a creature whose Master is the same One, spread through all.
games.why: the salok calls God the thaakur of jeea jant, Master of every living being, present within each one.

practice: Find a living thing you can see or hear, a bird outside, a houseplant, a pet, a fly on the window, even a picture of an animal you love, and watch its breathing, its movement, the way it pays attention to its world.
Then hold the thought quietly: the same Master, the same life. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as you watch.

wordCard.voice: Thaakur, lord or master: its salok calls God thaakur of jeea jant, Master of every living thing, and says the One is spread through them all.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: thaakur, lord or master; in the salok, thaakuraa, Lord of all beings.

carryVoice: Your line: lord of all. Every breathing thing, one Master. That's day five hundred twenty-two.
